Beyond the compute bottleneck: Maximizing the ROI of AI accelerators with purpose-built storage

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there’s a lot more to AI infrastructure than just buying accelerators.
  • To optimize your accelerators’ TCO, you need to keep them fully occupied.
  • Organizations are eager to move their AI initiatives forward, but preventing idle compute requires a purpose-built approach to data I/O.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VP, Product Management, Storage.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Industry observers note that there’s a lot more to AI infrastructure than just buying accelerators. Indeed, the infrastructure mandate for enterprise AI has shifted from acquiring accelerators to keeping them fully utilized. Next to these expensive accelerators, storage accounts for only a small sliver of total AI spend. However, having the wrong storage in place can put the rest of your committed compute capital at risk.

To optimize your accelerators’ TCO, you need to keep them fully occupied. Very often, the challenge here is data I/O. If accelerators sit waiting to read or write data, you’re wasting money. Across the industry, insufficient storage throughput has become a primary impediment to AI success, starving models of the data they need. And the problem is only going to get worse. Gartner predicts enterprises will deploy over 150,000 agents in the next few years, so the I/O bottleneck and the challenge of orchestrating storage for agentic fleets will only compound.

Organizations are eager to move their AI initiatives forward, but preventing idle compute requires a purpose-built approach to data I/O. With the demands of AI, standard enterprise storage — even a system optimized for fast analytics — will inevitably suffer from bottlenecks that leave compute resources twiddling their proverbial thumbs.

The most common architectural misstep we see is treating AI as a single, general-purpose workload. In reality, the physical movement of data transforms across the AI lifecycle, creating distinct I/O profiles based on how models consume and generate information:.

In model training, clusters read datasets at high throughput, but pause regularly to write checkpoints to record their state in event of a failure. When thousands of GPUs attempt to save this data in a single, simultaneous burst, standard storage architectures stall. That’s especially true of traditional cloud storage, which is engineered for durability. Writing checkpoints triggers thousands of administrative database transactions to safely record the files, bogging down the system, choking the network, and freezing the entire GPU cluster until the save is complete. Furthermore, saving the data is only one of the problems: If a server fails, slow storage turns a routine checkpoint recovery into a multi-hour delay, leaving expensive accelerators sitting completely idle.

According to recent reports, inference, conversely, is real-time and latency-sensitive. As AI services scale to meet user demand, inference clusters constantly load and unload petabyte-scale model repositories quickly. In this case, a slow storage system can leave GPUs in a “cold start” as they wait for data. Also, many models now process context windows that exceed 100,000 tokens, filling up accelerator memory. Without a high-speed external cache to offload this context, when a user asks the next question, the accelerator must recalculate previous inputs, wasting compute on redundant operations.

To solve these I/O challenges and keep expensive accelerators busy, organizations need compute, networking, and storage to be deeply integrated.

Recent findings suggest that as industry analysts have noted, enterprise customers gain a unique performance advantage because Google Cloud runs on the exact same storage foundation as Google's own consumer products. This foundation is built on Colossus—the planet-scale distributed file system powering Google Search, YouTube, and Gemini. Because this shared infrastructure supports billions of consumers daily, its reliability is continuously proven against the extreme traffic and hardware demands of Google's global consumer services. As a result, today, nine out of the world’s ten leading AI frontier model labs run on Google Cloud infrastructure because we deliver the throughput and performance they require to innovate. In fact, we spent the last two years co-designing our storage architecture directly with these frontier labs as well as with Google's own foundation model teams.

Recent findings suggest that for large-scale training on object storage, our architecture ensures workloads don’t have to wait on data, and successfully absorbs peak bandwidth demands. For real-time inference, enterprise platform companies like Salesforce AI Research leverage our architecture to serve complex agentic inference workloads with up to 40% fewer GPUs. We deliver these outcomes through two distinct, purpose-built storage solutions:.

According to recent reports, cloud Storage Rapid: For organizations that have standardized on cloud-native object storage, Cloud Storage Rapid provides Colossus scale and performance directly to accelerators, so they can use the data stored on object storage in their AI workflows. This eliminates the need to migrate data into separate, specialized storage silos to achieve the performance that AI workloads require. A single Rapid bucket pushes the boundaries of object storage, delivering up to 15 TB/s of throughput and 20 million queries per second with sub-millisecond latency. This makes it a strong fit for streaming large training datasets and recovering checkpoints without bottlenecking the network. For bursty workloads such as model loading across multiple locations, Rapid Cache acts as a read accelerator that co-locates active data directly with TPU and GPU clusters. With no code changes, Rapid Cache delivers up to 2.5 TB/s of aggregate read throughput, taking idle cold-start times from hours to minutes.

In a recent development, google Cloud Managed Lustre: For demanding AI and HPC workloads that need a parallel file system, there’s Google Cloud Managed Lustre. Built in partnership with DDN, Managed Lustre provides up to 10 TB/s of throughput per instance, absorbing the intense read-write bursts of synchronous checkpointing and reinforcement learning, so that your expensive accelerators remain fully saturated.To help organizations scale their workloads without breaking budgets, Managed Lustre’s fresh Dynamic Tier delivers more Lustre for less by consolidating hot and cold data into a single namespace, eliminating traditional caching performance cliffs. Finally, Managed Lustre Cloud Storage Mirror reduces the downtime and operational friction inherent in manual data transfers. Instead of you having to write custom scripts that leave expensive compute clusters waiting on files, it automatically synchronizes datasets in the background so they are ready before training begins.

This purpose-built storage foundation is already powering customers’ most demanding AI workloads, helping them extract maximum return on investment from their compute resources.

Thinking Machines Lab utilizes Cloud Storage Rapid Cache to stabilize read throughput peaks above 1.8 TB/s and achieve an 89% cache hit ratio, completely eradicating rate-limiting surge errors across their multi-region architecture.

Shopify deployed 50+ unique Rapid Caches across their worldwide footprint, achieving over 2 TB/s peak throughput and up to a 90% latency reduction from their baseline to meet the data demands of their growing compute scale.

Salesforce AI Research uses Managed Lustre as a high-throughput, low-latency external cache to keep their GPUs fully saturated, driving substantial performance gains for LLM inference over previous hardware generations.

Atlassian adopted Managed Lustre on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to turn preemption interruptions into quick five-minute restores, delivering nearly 5x higher throughput and boosting their GPU utilization by 70% compared to NVMe-based systems.

Harmonic relies on Managed Lustre to train mathematical reasoning models, eliminating 50% of experiment interruptions, cutting startup times in half, and increasing data retrieval speeds by 15x.

Sources indicate that when advising AI Infrastructure teams designing their stack today, our guidance is straightforward. First, evaluate your token economics rather than just legacy storage metrics. If your chips are waiting on data, optimizing storage is a cost-effective and efficient remedy. Second, avoid creating separate copies of data for every new workload; keep your primary data in a unified foundation and move it to the right tier as needed. Finally, while AI performance grabs the headlines, you can’t create your AI strategy on infrastructure built for a different era. At the same time, AI infrastructure needs enterprise-grade reliability, built-in security, and automated cost discipline for optimized TCO.

Sources indicate that the future of enterprise AI belongs to organizations that can turn their data into action. Google Cloud enables you to match the speed of your storage to the speed of your compute, so that you maximize your compute investments.

Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (180 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.20794v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide semantic features for uplift estimation, but treatment-revealing text can induce prediction shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization (LULR) to address this risk. With the LLM encoder frozen, LULR penalizes dependence between the causal head's trainable shared representation and treatment while retaining separate outcome heads. The penalty uses a variational approximation to the contrastive log-ratio upper bound (CLUB) of mutual information, targeting treatment dependence rather than generic parameter shrinkage. Controlled proxy experiments provide exploratory evidence of improved ranking scores under injected treatment information relative to no regularization and the tested weight-decay setting. Structured-only benchmarks show modest, dataset-dependent effects. On an industrial pricing randomized controlled trial, mean offline lift@0.3 is 0.258 for LULR, compared with 0.106 for the same-backbone baseline. A separate one-week online A/B test of the complete deployed pricing policy records 5.45% higher sales volume and 1.91% higher gross merchandise value than the control arm. These short-term policy-level gains do not isolate the regularizer's effect.

arXiv:2611.19292v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Weight-space programming fixes every parameter of a feed-forward network by hand, with no gradient descent anywhere in the construction. Every demonstration so far starts from a target function handed to the model as a rule system, making it a compilation problem. A supervised dataset withholds that specification, so the procedure must do the statistical inference itself and then express the result in the parameterisation it was given. We ask whether a large language model can do both. It is shown a small dataset in full, with the architecture of a feed-forward network, and writes out every weight and bias as a literal number, with no optimizer, no gradient, no code execution, and no chance to evaluate it first. Each construction is sealed and pre-registers its expected score. The graded suite runs from two toy problems, through nine synthetic problems disguised by a hidden rotation, to the classical benchmarks and one real engineering regression. The frozen network matches the closed-form optimum wherever that optimum is linear, reaches the irreducible error of the generating process on three rungs where it is not, and beats every fitted baseline on two of those, including the same architecture trained by gradient descent. It fails on two rungs, both times because the structure to be found is oblique to the coordinates it analysed. Three further constructors separate two failure modes a single score conflates: one returns no parameter vector at all on the hardest rungs, another delivers everywhere while writing networks worse than predicting the mean. One of those failures proves avoidable: another constructor solves the oblique-hinge rung by a margin that survives multiple-comparison correction. What predicts whether the hidden layer earns its keep is the training error of a linear separator, which the composite complexity index misses.

#8554. Breaking: Sovereign AI in Europe: New ways to control your AI stack

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1130 w)

Breaking: Sovereign AI in Europe: New ways to control your AI stack

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today in Brussels, public sector leaders, policymakers and partners are meeting at the Sovereign AI Summit to discuss how to build the next decade of Europe's public services, healthcare, and finance with AI under European control.
  • Achieving that goal takes more than deciding where data is stored.
  • Will choosing more control mean settling for less capable AI?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VP & GM, Regulated & Sovereign Cloud.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

According to recent reports, today in Brussels, public sector leaders, policymakers and partners are meeting at the Sovereign AI Summit to discuss how to build the next decade of Europe's public services, healthcare, and finance with AI under European control. We're here with our European partners to help deliver it.

Achieving that goal takes more than deciding where data is stored. When we talk with European organizations, we hear four common questions from them:.

Will choosing more control mean settling for less capable AI?

Who can access our data, and can we prove to regulators that our controls work?

Will the value that organizations create with AI stay in Europe?

How can we keep AI running reliably?

Industry observers note that in May 2025, we introduced a portfolio of sovereign cloud offerings for customers to match their desired level of control to each workload. In February, we set out the commitments behind that portfolio, covering local investment, operational continuity, customer control over data, and open technology.

Today, we’re building on these commitments. Gemini models are coming to Google Cloud Dedicated, our partner-operated cloud, expanding model choice beyond the open models already available in the model garden. We are also announcing upcoming capabilities for cryptographic key control and compliance, and new work with European software companies and startups.

Sovereignty is not one-size-fits-all, so Sovereign Cloud from Google offers three ways to run a workload. First, Google Cloud Data Boundary applies data residency, access, and encryption controls on our public cloud. A second option is Google Cloud Dedicated, which is operated by an independent local partner on isolated infrastructure. And finally, Google Distributed Cloud runs in a customer's own data center connected or fully air-gapped.

Select Gemini models are already available in Google Cloud with a commitment to perform machine-learning processing of customer data in-region for these models, including within the EU. It is also available with Google Distributed Cloud. And with today’s announcement that Gemini is coming to Google Cloud Dedicated, organizations that require a locally operated cloud will be able to use it there too.

Many teams also want open models, or models they have tuned themselves. In France, S3NS has made managed model serving and inference generally available on PREMI3NS, its cloud built on Google Cloud Dedicated. Teams can deploy open models from providers such as Mistral and Google through Model Garden, or bring their own models. S3NS operates the environment, designed so the deployed models and prompts remain within the PREMI3NS environment under S3NS's control.

Recent findings suggest that for many European organizations, data access, encryption key access and services access dictate their sovereignty posture. On our public cloud, customers can already see when Google personnel access their data and why, approve or deny that access with Access Transparency, Access Approval, and Key Access Justifications. Customers who want  more control can hold their encryption keys outside Google Cloud, which enables them to deny access to their data for any reason. Together, these controls help ensure the customer controls any and all access to their data.

In a recent development, when customers hold keys outside Google Cloud, every key request has to travel to an external system, which can add latency and availability risk. Confidential External Key Management (cEKM), presently in preview, is designed to remove that trade-off: Customers, or their chosen local partner, hold and control access to the root keys outside Google Cloud, while key operations run inside a hardware-attested Confidential Computing environment designed to run with the low latency and reliability that data-intensive workloads, including AI, demand.

Customers can also ask trusted local partners to hold their keys external from Google infrastructure. A newly introduced partnership with Telefónica in Spain (currently in preview) expands customer options beyond existing European partnerships France, Germany, Italy, Spain.

Auditing sovereignty controls and requirements is not only difficult, it often requires engineering effort. To help make audits smoother, we are introducing Data Boundary frameworks that map local and regional regulatory requirements to enforced, auditable controls. A framework for Switzerland is available today, and a framework for the EU's Digital Operational Resilience (DORA) Act is planned for financial services organizations.

With Audit Manager, customers can start from a ready-made framework, adapt it to their own policies, and give auditors continuous, machine-readable evidence, designed to keep customer data within their designated boundary.

Sovereignty also depends on who operates the technology, and whether the value it creates stays local. That's why we work with European companies at every layer: those that operate the cloud, those that build software for it, and the startups that will build what comes next.

According to recent reports, google Cloud Dedicated is designed so that the local partner controls the environment, can block software updates in exceptional circumstances, and can keep operating for up to 12 months in the unlikely scenario that its Dedicated instance connection to Google is severed. These design choices sit alongside the commitments we made in February, including that should Google receive an order from a national government to suspend or terminate the provision of Google Cloud's operations provided from any country, we will seek to limit, modify, or object to any such order using all available legal avenues.

Recent findings suggest that in France, PREMI3NS from S3NS has achieved SecNumCloud 3.2 qualification from ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency. With Thales, we are extending Google Cloud Dedicated to Germany (currently in preview), to enable a sovereign hyperscale capability across the EU.

Regulated workloads often stall because the security, identity, and monitoring tools that teams depend on are not available in a sovereign environment. More than a dozen software vendors have now validated their products on Google Cloud Dedicated, including European providers such as Memority and Tsuga.

We also want to help the new companies and skills that AI is creating  to take root in Europe. The new Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI is an equity-free program that gives startups in regulated sectors support from Google engineers, mentorship, and access to local cloud providers.

We are continuing to build on the strategy we set in 2025: giving customers control that they can verify, a choice in  how they operate in the cloud and who operates the environment, and access to advanced AI regardless of your deployment choices. We will keep bringing more of our AI platform to partner-operated and on-premises environments, extending access and key controls to more services, and adding frameworks for more regulations, together with the European partners who operate these services.

To learn more, visit Sovereign Cloud from Google or talk to a sovereign specialist.

SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (214 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.15481v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.11010v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (GraphRAG) improves multi-hop question answering, but deployed systems pay costs that research comparisons rarely measure: model calls at query time, building the graph, and removing documents correctly. We present Lightfoot, a GraphRAG system in which every entity, link, fact and synonym edge is a deterministic function of per-passage extractions that carry chunk-level provenance. Retrieval makes no language-model call, indexing makes one per passage, and deleting a document is a database transaction with no model calls: 14 seconds for 10% of an 11,402-passage corpus, after which the graph is identical to a fresh index of the surviving documents. On a corpus of near-duplicate names, HippoRAG 2's capped synonym lists leave 565 fewer edges than a rebuild, while Lightfoot remains exact. Under identical extraction, embedding and answer models on held-out questions of MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, Lightfoot is competitive with HippoRAG 2: with Holm-corrected paired tests it is better on MuSiQue at recall@5 and recall@10 (+4.8 and +5.5 points) and on 2WikiMultiHopQA at recall@10 (+3.4), and tied on HotpotQA, while HippoRAG 2 keeps a non-significant 3.0-point edge at 2WikiMultiHopQA recall@2. Seeding the walk from entities named in the question accounts for most of the 2WikiMultiHopQA gain. Answers tie on all three datasets, and the retrieval pattern holds with three larger embedders, up to Qwen3-Embedding-8B. The gain is not the reranker's: with the same cross-encoder, dense retrieval trails Lightfoot by 9.3 and 17.8 points recall@5 on the two multi-hop sets. Lightfoot also builds the cheapest index, 26-31% below HippoRAG 2; LightRAG needed 2,187 model calls and 3.7 hours for the same deletion, and fast-graphrag cannot delete.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we’re announcing an open call for applications for the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI.
  • Industry observers note that today we’re announcing an open call for applications for the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI.
  • Artificial intelligence represents an estimated €1.2 trillion economic opportunity for Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we’re announcing an open call for applications for the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI. Available in Europe and Israel, this initiative supports startups that are building cutting-edge AI solutions for European regulatory environments. Artificial intelligence represents an estimated €1.2 trillion economic opportunity for Europe. To realize this potential, European enterprises and public institutions need to adopt advanced AI while also meeting crucial data governance requirements, including the EU AI Act, NIS2, DORA, and national frameworks such as SecNumCloud and BSI's cloud security and sovereignty principles. We want ambitious founders to build in Europe, with solutions made in Europe. For startups, digital sovereignty cannot mean settling for second-rate tools or getting locked into a single rigid stack. It means co-engineering with Europe's tech ecosystem so founders can scale on their own terms from day one: for instance combining frontier Gemini models, open-weight models like Gemma and Mistral, and verifiable data residency and cryptographic controls delivered with local European sovereign partners. How it works This equity-free, 15-week hybrid program includes virtual and in-person sessions connecting founders with Google engineers, regulatory experts, and local partners. Selected startups receive hands-on architectural mentorship, 1:1 pairing with Google Cloud engineers, and advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act Regulatory Sandboxes. Participants will gain direct support to deploy across Google Cloud’s tiered sovereign portfolio: Sovereign cloud infrastructure: From regional data controls and external key management (data boundary) to partner-operated clouds (such as S3NS in France and Thales in Germany) and fully air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments. Auditable, private AI: Fine-tuning and deploying open-weight models like the Gemma family (including MedGemma) in sovereign environments for verifiable control over data and operations. Ecosystem and investors access: Direct engagement with European sovereign cloud operators, system integrators, and institutional investors to compress enterprise sales cycles. Who should apply We are selecting a small, high-touch cohort of late-seed to post Series A startups headquartered across Europe and Israel with strong traction that use AI to handle sensitive, regulated workloads. We’re specifically seeking startups focused on: Government and public service technologies including sovereign document processing, citizen service portals, municipal operations, smart utilities, and civic emergency grids (defense applications excluded). Healthcare and life sciences including clinical trial analytics, electronic health records (EHR/EHDS), diagnostic copilots, and hospital operations that meet compliance requirements for GDPR and the European Health Data Space. Regulated finance including credit risk modeling, anti-money laundering pipelines, fraud detection, credit underwriting pipelines, and claims processing. Cybersecurity and data trust including enterprise threat detection and response, supply chain security, vulnerability scanning, and civilian IT infrastructure protection. If you’re a founder building sovereign AI to power Europe’s digital autonomy, we want to help you scale your impact. You can apply on the Google for Startups Accelerator page. The deadline for applications is January 15th, 2027. Hear from past participants how the accelerator program helped supercharge their products: "In sovereign and regulated environments, proving tech works is only part of the challenge. Having direct access to Google Cloud engineers who understand these constraints can save a young manufacturer a great deal of time." Denise Williams, Managing Director, Dysplasia "If you are building deep-tech for regulated and sovereign markets, you cannot afford to build in isolation. The technical depth, mentorship, and validation you gain through the Accelerator cut through years of trial and error."  Maria Terzi, Co-Founder and CEO, Malloc "Building in regulated spaces requires expert guidance that flags hidden hurdles. This cohort provides the technical clarity and expert access needed to turn strict compliance into your greatest competitive advantage."  Gabriela Isas, Co-Founder and CEO, Good With "In regulated markets your customers will ask where data lives and how AI makes decisions. The Accelerator programme helps you build those answers into your architecture from day one."  Kartik Dabbiru, Founder and Chief Executive Officer, ComplyStream "Operating in regulated markets doesn't stop you from using frontier AI; it means designing for control from day one. The Accelerator programme helped us navigate that balance effectively." Juan Mir de Leonardo, Product Director, Connect by Circular-Lab.

Artificial intelligence represents an estimated €1.2 trillion economic opportunity for Europe. To realize this potential, European enterprises and public institutions need to adopt advanced AI while also meeting crucial data governance requirements, including the EU AI Act, NIS2, DORA, and national frameworks such as SecNumCloud and BSI's cloud security and sovereignty principles.

We want ambitious founders to build in Europe, with solutions made in Europe. For startups, digital sovereignty cannot mean settling for second-rate tools or getting locked into a single rigid stack. It means co-engineering with Europe's tech ecosystem so founders can scale on their own terms from day one: for instance combining frontier Gemini models, open-weight models like Gemma and Mistral, and verifiable data residency and cryptographic controls delivered with local European sovereign partners.

According to recent reports, this equity-free, 15-week hybrid program includes virtual and in-person sessions connecting founders with Google engineers, regulatory experts, and local partners. Selected startups receive hands-on architectural mentorship, 1:1 pairing with Google Cloud engineers, and advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act Regulatory Sandboxes.

Participants will gain direct support to deploy across Google Cloud’s tiered sovereign portfolio:.

Sovereign cloud infrastructure: From regional data controls and external key management (data boundary) to partner-operated clouds (such as S3NS in France and Thales in Germany) and fully air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments.

Auditable, private AI: Fine-tuning and deploying open-weight models like the Gemma family (including MedGemma) in sovereign environments for verifiable control over data and operations.

Ecosystem and investors access: Direct engagement with European sovereign cloud operators, system integrators, and institutional investors to compress enterprise sales cycles.

We are selecting a small, high-touch cohort of late-seed to post Series A startups headquartered across Europe and Israel with strong traction that use AI to handle sensitive, regulated workloads.

We’re specifically seeking startups focused on:.

Government and public service technologies including sovereign document processing, citizen service portals, municipal operations, smart utilities, and civic emergency grids (defense applications excluded).

Healthcare and life sciences including clinical trial analytics, electronic health records (EHR/EHDS), diagnostic copilots, and hospital operations that meet compliance requirements for GDPR and the European Health Data Space.

Regulated finance including credit risk modeling, anti-money laundering pipelines, fraud detection, credit underwriting pipelines, and claims processing.

Cybersecurity and data trust including enterprise threat detection and response, supply chain security, vulnerability scanning, and civilian IT infrastructure protection.

According to recent reports, if you’re a founder building sovereign AI to power Europe’s digital autonomy, we want to help you scale your impact. You can apply on the Google for Startups Accelerator page. The deadline for applications is January 15th, 2027.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.09271v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating proposal, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison.

arXiv:2611.06374v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI's inflection point is a fountain of risks for digital platforms, as those in control of global platforms cede control of the algorithms, membership and content to AI: (i) AI control of global platforms used by the majority of humanity; (ii) unaccountable AI agents operating anonymously, possibly masquerading as humans, serving unknown masters with unknown goals; and (iii) unattributed deepfakes generated by anonymous AI, which people cannot distinguish from genuine content. Here, we propose to corral these AI risks with grassroots contracts, a digital incarnation of a two-centuries old notion of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon: a social contract that can be freely adopted by any group of people, where groups bound by the same contract can union by mutual consent, possibly into a single global union. Grassroots contracts are realised by grassroots platforms, person-to-person platforms owned, operated and governed by their participants. We developed, with AI, a methodology to compile grassroots contracts to working smartphone apps. We present grassroots contracts for a social graph with accountable AI agents and for a social network with digital provenance, and working smartphone apps that implement the two, and show how they corral these risks: (i) grassroots platforms are not controlled by a third party who may cede control to AI; (ii) AI agents are introduced with accountability: similarly to cars, their manufacturers are accountable for manufacturing defects and their operators for reckless operation; and (iii) every item carries the signatures of its author and of every agent that forwarded it, so creators and forwarders of harmful content are accountable and culpable. Much work remains for grassroots apps to be competitive with incumbent global platforms; but perhaps now this could be achieved with some AI-months rather than with incalculably-many person-years.

Skill erosion, individual memory and the reversibility of AI adoption

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (238 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.04886v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills needed for future work. We consider a population of agents who perform a task either with their own skill or with the help of AI. Agents tend to imitate more successful peers, and their skills evolve in time: improving with practice and eroding with reliance on AI. We study, analytically and with simulations, the collective consequences of AI adoption. We show that the mechanism of skill erosion makes adoption bistable and that the long-term behaviour of the population depends on how skills are distributed: populations with the same adoption and mean skill can reach opposite asymptotic states, depending on how expertise is shared between AI customers and non-users. A deterministic description that follows the mean skills of the two groups and the variance of skills among non-users predicts the outcome of individual runs as accurately as the simulations allow, whereas the means alone are not sufficient. We also consider the situation when the benefit of AI improves in time. In that case, adoption can jump abruptly, and a temporary increase in benefit, such as in a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its original value. Skill erosion therefore creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

Large language model agents can now retrieve materials data, operate simulation codes, and close design-synthesis-characterization loops with autonomous laboratories. However, extending these agents with latest capabilities, keeping long-running tasks on track, and letting them learn from past tasks and user feedback remain difficult. Here we present MatOS, an agent operating system for materials research with three core components: (1) a layered scientific asset graph that organizes data, knowledge, tools, skills, roles, and workflows as reusable assets; (2) a stateful adaptive workflow that runs tasks as explicit execution graphs with scientific checks, so that they can be resumed and traced; and (3) evidence-driven asset evolution, which revises these assets from execution records and user feedback. In eight research cases, MatOS narrowed more than 30 million candidate structures to 97 solid-electrolyte candidates, identified 89 halide variants with higher computed conductivity than their parent structures, linked the force errors of 11 pretrained interatomic potentials to local atomic environments, and supported two new methods that reduce errors by 3.1% and 13.6% relative to their baselines. These results show that organizing research capabilities as reusable, evolving assets enables agents to carry out long, multistage materials studies. arXiv:2610.31276v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Long-horizon coding agents can observe a failure and generate a plausible critique yet continue along the same incorrect trajectory. We call this the Critique-to-Action Handoff Gap. We introduce RIPPLE, a recovery-oriented training framework that internalizes process-level guidance into a single self-recovering policy. A prefix-only teacher provides evidence-grounded recovery supervision without access to future actions or terminal outcomes. After lightweight distillation, reinforcement learning assigns stage-specific credit to reflection triggering, diagnosis, and corrective action. Local validity signals gate trajectory advantages so that intermediate recovery decisions do not indiscriminately inherit terminal outcomes. Across four repository-level software-engineering benchmarks, RIPPLE improves the base policy by an arithmetic mean of 4.8 score points, with no auxiliary critic at deployment. Controlled ablations isolate the benefits of local, stage-aligned credit, and matched-prefix interventions show that critique semantics affect subsequent correction. Recovery gains concentrate where the prefix contains sufficient diagnostic evidence and the repository state remains reversible within the remaining budget.

Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (266 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2610.26836v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls demonstrates that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.

Breaking: ABACUS: Program-Guided Multistep Reasoning over Frozen Judgment Models

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (197 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.25963v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Judgment models answer semantic questions by scoring a finite set of candidate outcomes. Can reusable programs turn these local decisions into powerful multistep reasoning? We introduce \method, a framework that jointly constructs judgment schemas and composition programs for frozen judgment models. A generative teacher designs the procedure offline; the judgment model resolves local semantic questions online, and the saved program composes its decisions into an answer. We study three allocations of design effort between humans and the teacher, focusing on construction through a shared interface. We instantiate the framework with Kev. On three selected MAJOR-Bench Hard tasks, nine independently constructed programs solve all 450 executions of 150 development inputs. A separate deployment study freezes three programs after development-set reference-agreement refinement and evaluates them on 600 held-out questions. These programs achieve near-perfect 99.67\% macro accuracy, versus 64.00\% for direct Kev and 68.80\% for final-answer-only Qwen3.5-4B. They attain comparable observed accuracy to Qwen's unrestricted response policy (99.07\%) with an \textbf{8.43-fold online speedup}: 0.255 versus 2.150 seconds per question. These results show how reusable programs can substantially expand the reasoning capability of a compact judgment model while keeping its parameters fixed.

Tech Report: Screening LLM Judges Without Ground Truth: A Preliminary Evaluation of an AI Dental Hygiene Coach

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (270 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.24335v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Evaluating a fine-tuned coaching model with expert graders is slow and expensive, and an LLM judge cannot be trusted without ground truth. We present a staged pipeline that screens candidate LLM judges and student models before expert review, using explicit decision rules at each stage: judge output audit, similarity with hosted judges, bias checks, and decision robustness. We demonstrate it on an AI dental hygiene coach. The case study uses synthetic, clinically unvalidated training and reference data to demonstrate the operation of the pipeline, rather than to establish the clinical performance of the resulting models. Two fine-tuned small language models (Granite-4.1-8B and Qwen3-8B), each trained at three data sizes, were scored on seven metrics by five judges (three local, two hosted). Two local judges, Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B-it, were not distinguishable from the agreement between the hosted judges on six of seven metrics by rank correlation, and Qwen3.8-27B was the most similar to the hosted judges overall. No judge met our criterion for favoring its own model family or training-data source. The student comparison did not separate the two models on any metric under the pipeline's rule, so the choice of Granite-4.1-8B, which led in 29 of 35 judge-by-metric cells, is a lean that depends partly on truncated Qwen3-8B outputs. The pipeline also surfaced problems that raw scores hid, including the truncated outputs and hallucination flags from one hosted judge that no other judge corroborated. No dental hygiene expert has graded these responses, so the findings are preliminary and the pipeline's final stage, anchoring to expert judgement, is proposed but not performed.

#8520. A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (241 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

A Conditional No-Hair Theorem for Transformers: How Language Models Forget Their Prompt

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (241 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2610.24133v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A black hole retains only a few conserved charges of the matter it formed from. We are inspired to make the analogy and we ask how much an autoregressive transformer retains of its prompt after generating $t$ tokens. For two prompts followed by the same continuation, the difference of their hidden states decays approximately as a power law $t^{-\alpha}$, where $\alpha=1$ is the rate at which a fixed prompt's share of uniform attention shrinks. Beyond the first layers, trained models forget faster ($\alpha\approx0.55$--$0.7$) than untrained ones of the same architecture ($\alpha\approx0.2$--$0.5$). For finite-depth pre-LN softmax transformers with bounded attention logits and non-degenerate pre-norm activations, we prove that this offset is $O\big(P(\log t)^{L-1}/t\big)$ for prompt length $P$ and depth $L$: the prompt's direct influence is diluted as the context grows, and \emph{relay} through continuation tokens adds only logarithmic factors. Conditional on the generated text, the prompt's influence on the next token thus vanishes. The bound fixes only the asymptotic shape and is uninformative at the lengths we measure in trained networks; an exactly solvable linear relay model reveals that it cannot be improved and accounts for the untrained curves. Cancelling the dilution with a logit bias on the prompt stops the decay early in training, and training suppresses relay by about one billion tokens, before attention sinks form. A toolkit that measures $\alpha$ for any Hugging Face causal language model is publicly available.

Agentic In-Context Learning: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn in Closed-Loop Interaction?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (196 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2610.23051v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The learning algorithm view of in-context learning (ICL) studies how fixed-parameter Transformers learn from supplied examples. Language model agents extend this setting through interaction: their actions determine what evidence enters context next. We call this regime Agentic In-Context Learning (Agentic ICL). Existing studies largely depend on externally supplied contexts or reward-bearing interaction histories, while work on general tool-using agents lacks a learning algorithm view. We represent an interactive learner by its state, update, and decision rule, covering active learning, bandits, and online reinforcement learning (RL). For expressivity, we construct causal Transformers that approximate these algorithms over a finite horizon, and bound the resulting loss in return. For training, we characterize when optimizing process rewards preserves behavior that maximizes the final outcome. Distillation experiments show that Transformers can learn to execute three representative recursions. We then train models from outcome or process rewards without oracle action or state targets, as in RL post-training. Different rewards yield distinct decision policies. Improving the alignment of process supervision with outcome-optimal action preferences shifts learned decisions accordingly. Such behavioral differences persist in a pretrained language model across textual paraphrases.

Breaking: Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (190 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2610.22155v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Real-time interaction requires agents to perceive evolving environments and act under temporal constraints, yet existing evaluations of real-time streaming models focus on conversational quality and streaming perception, leaving effective action under strict temporal constraints untested. We introduce Realtime-Bench, a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success. Under Wall Clock, where environments advance according to actual inference latency, the best success rate reaches only 44% and the best Pass^3 is only 36%, demonstrating that real-time interaction remains challenging. To separate serving latency from models' real-time streaming capability, we compare Wall Clock with Paused Clock, which removes inference delays as an idealized reference, and introduce Token Clock, which advances simulated time according to generated token counts, testing temporal awareness independently of physical serving speed. We find that temporal costs limit success in evolving environments and that higher reasoning effort has mixed effects under time pressure, reflecting a trade-off between decision quality and timely execution. Based on these results, we discuss future directions for improving real-time multimodal models, including adaptive reasoning with temporal awareness and continuous perception and action.

Latest Update: Reliable Self-Evolution with Imperfect Proxy Rewards

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (202 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

In a recent development, arXiv:2610.02975v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based self-evolving search is a promising approach to scientific discovery. However, high-fidelity evaluation of every candidate is prohibitively expensive in some domains. Self-evolving systems in such settings therefore rely on low-cost but imperfect proxy rewards, which may assign high scores to infeasible candidates. These false positives may contaminate both the final output and the feedback used to guide subsequent generations. This motivates statistically calibrated reward intervals for more reliable self-evolving search. We propose Conformal Interval-Driven Self-Evolution (CISE), which constructs candidate-specific reward intervals using conditional conformal inference and iteration-wise online density-ratio estimation. CISE uses conservative interval-based rewards for evolutionary feedback and returns candidates only when all required property intervals lie entirely within their respective feasible regions. We derive fixed-iteration coverage results under explicit assumptions of independence and covariate shift. We evaluate CISE on three self-evolving search tasks in materials science. In our experiments, all candidates returned by CISE are true positives under high-fidelity evaluation, whereas the baselines return more candidates but include false positives. These results highlight the value of a smaller, more precise shortlist when downstream validation budgets are limited. Our repository is available at https://github.com/MLAI-Yonsei/CISE.git.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2610.02405v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automated terminal-agent training relies on generated environments and verifiers to turn open-ended interaction into reward. Yet a runnable Docker image and executable test suite do not guarantee that the resulting reward is faithful, informative, or even attributable to agent behavior. We present a pipeline that generates containerized terminal tasks and their executable verifiers, and use it to demystify failure modes in task generation and live-environment evaluation. Our analysis separates four requirements that are often conflated: structural validity, verifier faithfulness, policy solvability, and infrastructure reliability. In a GRPO training of Qwen3.5-9B, it overfits on a relatively easy dataset within 20 steps. Conversely, in a controlled Qwen3.5-9B comparison, adding hard tasks lowers mean rollout pass@2 from 81.3% to 20.6%, restoring informative failures without changing the training configuration. We further identify near-duplicate task generation, incomplete anti-shortcut safeguards, Dockerfile failures, asynchronous pass@k bias, and concurrency-induced environment errors as distinct threats to measurement. These findings should motivate the community for a terminal agent specific evaluation harness that pairs structural checks and rollout-derived solvability with extensive verifier audits.

A ten-task probe suite gives each mechanism a reason to fire and reports where the change reaches the artifact, including one mechanism that cuts the signal it protects. Disabling five of six completion-time checks costs 0.152 of the artifact score on eighteen held-out tasks, three replications per cell (95% CI [+0.064, +0.246], Holm p = 0.014). On a 288-cell matrix the harness reaches 0.886 against 0.631, 0.479 and 0.405 for three open scaffolds, and on {\tau} 2 -bench it ranks first or tied first in all three domains against the arms evaluated.Tasks, scorer, source and every per-cell result are public.

arXiv:2609.36777v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Frontier coding agents can now write and execute code that authors 3D environments, but whether they reliably understand 3D structure and precisely control scene state remains unclear. The generated 3D scene is a persistent, executable artifact: a convincing render can hide incorrect spatial relations, intersecting objects, or unintended modifications. We introduce Code4Scene, a benchmark of 170 Unreal Engine cases built from human-assembled scenes that evaluates coding agents on two complementary settings under a shared execution interface. Construction tests scene-level spatial reasoning from open-ended language specifications, where many realizations are valid; editing tests precise control of scene state, where the agent must recover the target scene from reference images while preserving everything else. Rather than scoring code or rendered views, Code4Scene evaluates the generated engine-native scene for task fulfillment, artifact integrity, and static physical validity, with edits additionally compared against withheld ground truth. Across 14 coding-agent systems on the 83-case public set, construction and editing performance are strongly correlated but not interchangeable (Spearman $\rho = 0.67$): Claude Fable 5.1 leads construction, Gemini 3.8 Flash leads editing. Spatial Composition is the weakest construction category for every agent, while editing remains imprecise: the best Repair F1 is only 0.562, and 34.2% of edits that fully recover the target still introduce unintended changes elsewhere in the scene. These results expose a gap between plausible 3D generation and reliable spatial reasoning and state control. The project webpage is at https://simworld.org/code4scene.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2609.33319v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A key challenge in physics diagram understanding is correctly associating visual information with the physical entities, relations, and conditions it describes. Even when a value, symbol, or other local element is accurately recognized, assigning it to the wrong entity or scope can distort the underlying physical premise and lead to incorrect reasoning. To systematically study this challenge, we introduce \textbf{PhysAlign}, a benchmark designed to assess whether multimodal models correctly associate information recognized from physics diagrams with its intended physical role. By disentangling visual recognition from physical-role assignment through localized probes and controlled variants, PhysAlign isolates correspondence errors from recognition failures. It contains 3,341 human-validated probes spanning 986 physics problems, enabling systematic evaluation of visual recognition and physical-role correspondence at scale. We further introduce five complementary evaluation metrics, including CAcc, GAcc, and JAcc, which provide a comprehensive assessment of models' ability to recognize diagram content, establish correct physical correspondences, and solve the underlying physics problem. Across our evaluated multimodal models, PhysAlign reveals a consistent gap between local visual recognition and physical-role grounding. Even when the queried content is correctly recognized, the conditional correspondence error rate remains 13.8\% for GPT-6-Astra and rises to about 50.6\% for InternVL3.5-8B. These findings indicate that strong perception alone does not ensure reliable physical interpretation, exposing a distinct grounding bottleneck that is largely hidden by answer-level accuracy and highlighting the need for future models to better align recognized visual evidence with its physical meaning.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2609.01852v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Persistent-memory agents can follow stale information despite current authoritative evidence. We study stale-evidence reliance across Qwen3 0.6/1.7/4/8B checkpoints using two controlled, action-scored suites: a Benefit suite requiring stored information and a Safety suite providing current evidence as static prompt text. We distinguish stale-value reliance from net accuracy loss relative to no memory. Benefit-suite reliance is 0.92-1.00 across checkpoints. In the Safety suite, larger checkpoints resist a plain stale note but incur substantial harm when it appears newer. A full $2\times2\times2\times2$ factorial manipulates label, recency, source authority, and position. Direct cross-size contrasts identify stronger recency effects in the larger tested checkpoints and a position-effect sign reversal within Qwen3. Metadata improves accuracy at all four checkpoints, with larger gains at 4B/8B; pre-resolution yields near-ceiling accuracy across all four. Llama-Instruct comparisons provide cross-family evidence for selected effects, while RGB and MisBench corroborate stale-value reliance. A framing control reveals that the failure extends beyond memory-labeled content. These results characterize cue-dependent vulnerability across tested checkpoints without isolating capability or evaluating a complete memory lifecycle.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2608.25986v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge graph (KG)-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) leverages structured knowledge to provide large language models (LLMs) with high-quality external information. Building on these works, recent studies have explored multimodal knowledge graphs (MMKGs) as knowledge bases for GraphRAG. This enables GraphRAG to integrate knowledge across multiple modalities, thereby further enhancing its performance. However, existing MMKG-based RAG methods generally follow a common pipeline in which different modalities are largely processed independently before being fused. As a result, textual context is only used to a limited extent during visual information extraction and subsequent multimodal knowledge fusion. This brings a semantic gap between images and text which limits the multimodal GraphRAG performance. To address this matter, we propose a novel framework for constructing a Context-Enhanced MMKG (CEMMKG) to better support multimodal GraphRAG. The proposed CEMMKG enriches each image with complementary textual context at both local and global scopes. Local context goes beyond the surrounding text by incorporating sentences that are semantically related to the image, while global context provides a summary of the entire document. We further introduce a multi-granularity design for the local context, allowing it to capture semantically relevant information at different levels of detail. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets validate that CEMMKG is effective in leveraging contextual information to improve MMKG-based RAG performance. Moreover, its effectiveness across different MMKG-based RAG methods demonstrates its broad applicability.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (262 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2608.08077v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are often deployed as embodied controllers for robotics, yet it remains unclear how well they can explore an environment, maintain an internal map, and ground safety-critical decisions in long-horizon sequential trajectories. In this work, we introduce EMRD, an evaluation framework that decouples spatial reasoning into four stages: Explore (what the agent observes), Map (what it records and where), Remember (what it retains), and Decide (whether its final choice is justified), scored across 18 stage-specific metrics. We use EMRD to evaluate eleven open- and closed-weight VLMs across 16 buildings under nominal conditions and three environmental stresses (darkness, smoke, and motion noise), where an embodied VLM explores unknown rooms, maps observed objects, and selects the safest gathering place. Open-weight models leave rooms unvisited in 95% of episodes and detect at most 51% of objects; closed-weight models explore more, though with an external memory (notepad), two of the three stop prematurely. Without external memory, most VLMs keep fewer of the objects they saw, especially in larger buildings. The start limits which rooms are explored, and open-weight models started in different rooms agree on the final room not significantly more often than chance. Moreover, these choices are biased by semantic priors: swapping a room's label is often enough to change the final choice. Finally, motion noise increases object position error (by 12-60% for closed-weight models), strong darkness lowers map recall by 28-31 percentage points, and dense smoke reduces seen objects by 25-39 points, while the choice among the rooms entered does not change significantly.

Breaking: Alternating Abduction and Planning over Temporal Dynamic Knowledge Graphs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (260 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2607.27287v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Knowledge graphs change over time, but the effects of actions on them are only partly stated: the ontology entails further consequences, facts that an action needs are often unknown, and an action may make the graph inconsistent. We study these problems for Temporal Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (TDKGs), that is, SROIQ knowledge bases whose actions are rules with delete/insert templates and whose events lie on an intrinsic timeline. We present three tools: temporal projection, the exact test of prepares; DDA (Direct-Derivation Abduction), which explains an observation by assuming its negation and negating what the reasoner newly derives; and APT (Abduction and Planning over TDKGs), which plans backwards from a goal, assumes the facts that the proposal needs but nobody stated, and lets DDA explain the assumptions, each explanation becoming a sub-goal, up to a depth bound. The tools use a SROIQ reasoner only through a small contract, so they depend neither on a particular reasoner nor on a particular data structure; they are designed for a reasoner that processes added and removed axioms incrementally. Change is treated without modal operators, on one linear timeline and without possible worlds, so decidability of projection follows from that of SROIQ. We prove that indirect effects are exactly the entailments of the updated state, that DDA and APT are sound and terminate, and that bounded planning is 2NExpTime-hard and in 3ExpTime. We compare the tools with hitting-set abduction, the solver CATS and classical planning, and run them on six benchmarks and five reasoners with identical results.

#8481. Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (194 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Test-Time Coverage: Test-Conditioned Data Curation for Deployment-Aware Learning

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2607.22697v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deployed AI systems are often trained from broad candidate data pools, necessitating data curation towards the deployment test distribution. However, standard data curation methods score training-side criteria rather than directly optimizing deployment match. We introduce TTCov (Test-Time Coverage), a data-level test-conditioned curation method that uses test-side information before training instead of updating model weights at inference. TTCov decomposes deployment-conditioned curation into coverage and distribution. To represent coverage, it builds a task Atlas, a collection of LLM-based atomic propositions (APs) describing deployment-relevant concepts, seeded from open task knowledge and expanded with unmatched APs extracted from unlabeled deployment samples. To represent distribution, it instantiates the matched deployment APs with their frequencies, yielding a Knowledge Atlas (K-Atlas) that operationalizes the deployment distribution as a curation target. TTCov then selects a budgeted training set whose deployment APs distribution approximates this target. We apply TTCov towards autonomous driving (AD), keeping adaptation off the inference path while selecting data with greater deployment-relevant coverage, closer K-Atlas matching, and stronger downstream end-to-end driving performance than data-curation baselines, including seamless adaptability to novel domains via city-to-city expansion. Code available at https://github.com/NVlabs/TTCov.

#8478. RL Post-Training Builds Compositional Reasoning Strategies

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (245 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

RL Post-Training Builds Compositional Reasoning Strategies

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (245 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2607.07646v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Does RL post-training merely amplify primitive skills already latent in a base model, or can it compose primitive skills into new higher-level strategies? We study this question in a fully observable rewrite-grammar environment where the pretraining distribution is known and every generated rewrite can be audited. A Transformer is pretrained on primitive symbol-rewrite chains and post-trained on a Trace-based reasoning task with only a binary final-answer reward. RL solves held-out problems that remain rarely solved by the pretrained model even under much larger sampling budgets, while rejection fine-tuning improves early but plateaus. Trace analysis shows that RL reorganizes primitive competence through a phased compositional mechanism: it first strengthens primitive reductions, then discovers valid composed procedures. These include sequential compositions, which collapse ordered chains of primitive contractions, and parallel compositions, which combine independent primitive contractions in a single step. The composed procedures are not isolated samples; they are reused and consolidated into a stable repertoire. Comparing RL with rejection fine-tuning shows that the key difference is not exploration volume but selectivity: RFT produces many shortcut-like rewrites, much of them invalid, whereas RL concentrates exploration into valid reusable structure. Pretraining ablations show that the emergence of compositional strategies is gated not by primitive exposure alone, but by whether pretraining organizes primitive competence into reduction procedures that RL can later compress. The base model provides weak procedural ingredients; RL builds them into reliable higher-level strategies.

Process Advantage Signal Shaping: Advantage Construction for Process-Supervised Reinforcement Learning in LLM Reasoners

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (189 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2606.29296v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dense process supervision provides local evaluations, but leaves open how these scores should become policy advantages. We introduce PASS (Process Advantage Signal Shaping), an advantage-construction method for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). PASS separately normalizes and fuses reward channels, constructs batch-shared credit units from variation in the fused score trace, and normalizes return-to-go by the remaining unit count. These operations connect feedback scale, credit resolution, and accumulation horizon in a single computation. We evaluate learned process reward model (PRM) feedback for mathematical reasoning and teacher-derived token feedback for multi-hop question answering (QA). Across seven mathematics benchmarks, PASS improves average pass@1 by 4.62 percentage points over outcome-only GRPO with approximately $2\%$ shorter responses. Matched comparisons with Step-GRPO and component ablations further support the choice of shared credit units and residual normalization. On multi-hop QA, PASS improves over process-signal controls across two normalizers; token-level ablations reveal an accuracy--length trade-off: token-level accumulation slightly favors pass@1, while PASS achieves higher pass@8/16 with shorter responses. The results establish the conversion from local process scores to policy advantages as a consequential design choice across distinct supervision sources.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Latent Goal Prediction from Language for Model-Based Planning

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (222 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2606.20627v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable agents to plan in latent space by imagining the outcomes of candidate actions, yet task specification remains a bottleneck. Visual targets provide precise local gradients but poor distant guidance, while language is flexible yet limited by noisy cross-modal alignment or dependence on distinct large generative models. We introduce LAGO (Latent Goal Prediction from Language), a hierarchical world model in which a single predictor both forecasts action-conditioned dynamics and grounds language instructions as sequences of intermediate latent subgoals, training both modes with a single regression objective over a shared latent space. At each planning step, LAGO predicts a sequence of latent subgoals from a language instruction and optimizes an action sequence using a soft-minimum alignment cost that rewards subgoal proximity without enforcing a rigid path. Subgoals are repredicted as the agent's state evolves, turning a single long-horizon instruction into a sequence of locally tractable objectives. Across environments spanning navigation and manipulation, LAGO outperforms flat and hierarchical image-goal planners, with the largest gains on long-horizon navigation with curved, hazard-constrained paths, where it more than doubles the success rate of a goal-conditioned behavior cloning policy trained on the same demonstrations. Grounding language in the world model's own latent space also outperforms vision-language reward models, including one that looks with ground-truth dynamics.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Rhythm of the Deep: Two-tier acoustic organization of sperm-whale codas from click waveforms to coda sequences

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2606.16084v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Sperm-whale codas are usually described by the number and timing of their clicks. These measures reveal patterns in whale communication, but do not describe how individual clicks sound. We ask what click waveforms add beyond timing and how acoustic information is organized within codas and across sequences of codas. We analyze 1,952 codas, using frozen audio encoders to identify recurring forms of clicks and whole codas independently. Direct spectral and envelope measurements then test whether the click forms differ in recorded sound. Within codas, click-form composition improves the measured prediction of whole-coda form beyond timing alone. Click spacing also remains related to whole-coda sound when the same click forms are present. Neighboring click forms help predict the next click in the annotated sample, although their order does not improve the tested classification of whole codas. Across recorded sequences, the second preceding whole-coda form improves prediction beyond the immediately preceding form. The gain exceeds two broad first-order references, but stricter controls do not establish a general higher-order rule. Together, these findings show different organizing relationships at the two scales. Within codas, click sound and rhythmic spacing help distinguish complete vocalizations. Across codas, earlier whole-coda forms help predict what follows.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2606.05464v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Verifiable reward training has improved mathematical and coding reasoning, but these domains capture only part of step-by-step decision making. Many real-world tasks require finding a high-value feasible blueprint among many valid alternatives. We introduce OPT*, a scalable family of optimization-style tasks for training and evaluating LLM step-by-step optimization-like reasoning along a complexity axis: each task provides a feasibility checker and evaluator, while a complexity parameter expands the search space without requiring latest human labels. This motivates studying these tasks in two regimes: (i) solver-guided online policy optimization, which uses a solver as a value oracle for partial states and applies rank-based reward shaping to reinforce better next steps, and (ii) search-based offline RL when such solvers are unavailable. Theoretically, we relate success in large search spaces to the information a reasoner extracts per unit of search budget. Empirically, we ablate the ingredients that make search efficient on OPT* and show that training on OPT* improves step-by-step optimization-like reasoning.

arXiv:2605.25446v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Routine electrocardiogram (ECG) reports offer scalable supervision for cardiovascular representation learning. In this retrospective study, we pretrained CardioLoom, a report-guided ECG foundation model, on 2,781,289 ECG-report pairs from 1,298,359 patients. Downstream development used a separate cohort of 721,317 ECGs from 233,798 patients. Evaluation covered 89 targets, with external testing in nine cohorts. Across 45 internal ECG diagnoses, macro area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.624 versus 0.615 for DeepECG-SSL. Across 203 external ECG evaluations, corresponding means were 0.425 and 0.424. Using labels from 10% of training patients, CardioLoom achieved macro-AUPRC 0.559, exceeding supervised training with all labels (0.549). For heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, AUPRCs were 0.690, 0.641 and 0.677 in Zhongshan, Shiyuan and BIDMC. Cardiac amyloidosis screening yielded 4.5% positive predictive value using a threshold targeting 99% specificity in validation. Report-guided pretraining supported label-efficient ECG diagnosis, with variable transfer across echocardiographic phenotypes.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2605.09079v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Despite surpassing human performance across mathematics, coding, and other knowledge-intensive tasks, large language models (LLMs) continue to struggle with causal reasoning. A core obstacle is the target data itself: causal systems are complex and often expressed in non-executable forms, while ground-truth answers to causal queries are inherently scarce. We introduce CauSim, a framework that turns causal reasoning from a scarce-label problem into a scalable supervised one. CauSim constructs increasingly complex causal simulators: executable structural causal models (SCMs), incrementally built by LLMs, that scale to globally complex systems while maintaining verifiable answers to causal queries. CauSim operates across representations by formalizing non-executable causal knowledge into code, enabling data augmentation, and translating executable SCMs into natural language, enabling supervision in previously difficult-to-supervise representations. We structure our research into two parts: (1) how to construct increasingly complex causal simulators, and (2) a systematic study of what CauSim enables, demonstrating generalization across representations, consistent gains from curriculum scaling and data volume, LLM self-improvement through self-generated simulators, and data augmentation via formalization of existing domain knowledge.
